name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: “Happy Birthday to You”
items.fact: For decades a music company collected money whenever “Happy Birthday to You” was used in films or on TV. In 2015 a US judge ruled its copyright claim invalid, and it paid back $14 million.

items.name: The monkey selfie
items.fact: A macaque in Indonesia took selfies with a wildlife photographer's camera. An animal-rights group sued on the monkey's behalf, but in 2018 a US court ruled that animals cannot own copyright.

items.name: The Eiffel Tower at night
items.fact: The Eiffel Tower itself is free to photograph, but its night-time light show, added in 1985, is treated as a work of art. Selling photos of the tower lit up at night can need permission.

items.name: The silent track
items.fact: In 2002 a British composer put a one-minute silent track on an album, credited “Batt/Cage”. John Cage's publishers claimed it copied Cage's famous silent piece, 4′33″, and the row made headlines.

items.name: The one-copy album
items.fact: In 2015 the Wu-Tang Clan made just one copy of a new album and sold it for millions. By contract, the owner may play it to people for free but can't sell it commercially for 88 years.

items.name: Sherlock Holmes's feelings
items.fact: In 2020 Arthur Conan Doyle's estate sued Netflix because Sherlock Holmes showed feelings in a film. Most Holmes stories were out of copyright, but the estate said he only became warm in later ones.

items.name: Mike Tyson's tattoo
items.fact: The artist who designed Mike Tyson's face tattoo sued Warner Bros in 2011, because a copy of it appeared on an actor's face in The Hangover Part II. The two sides settled out of court.

items.name: Hot yoga poses
items.fact: A yoga teacher claimed copyright on his sequence of hot-yoga poses and sued studios that taught it. In 2015 a US appeals court ruled that a series of yoga poses can't be protected by copyright.

items.name: Radiohead's “Creep”
items.fact: Radiohead's hit “Creep” sounded so much like the Hollies' 1970s song “The Air That I Breathe” that its writers, Albert Hammond and Mike Hazlewood, were added to the song's list of writers.

items.name: Mickey Mouse goes free
items.fact: In January 2024 the very first Mickey Mouse, from the cartoon Steamboat Willie, lost its copyright protection in the US. Within days, several horror films starring that Mickey were announced.

fakes.name: The handball celebration
fakes.fact: In 2017 a Danish handball player registered copyright on his goal celebration, a little rowing dance. When a video game copied it, a court in Copenhagen ordered the game company to pay him.

fakes.name: The blackbird ringtone
fakes.fact: A Norwegian nature recordist sued a phone maker because its ringtone used his recording of a blackbird. The court ruled that he owned the recording, but nobody could own the bird's song.

fakes.name: The whistling parrot
fakes.fact: In 2009 a Belgian court ruled that a parrot whistling a famous advertising jingle in a TV comedy show counted as a “performance”, so the show had to pay the jingle's composer.

fakes.name: The sandcastle in the brochure
fakes.fact: In 2013 a Dutch sand artist won a case against a holiday company that used photos of his sandcastle in its brochure. The judge said it was a sculpture, even though the sea destroyed it.

fakes.name: The snoring album
fakes.fact: A Swedish man released an album of his own snoring and sued a sleep app that used similar sounds. The court ruled that snoring is a natural noise, so nobody can own it.

fakes.name: The weather presenter's hands
fakes.fact: In 2011 an Austrian TV weather presenter claimed copyright on her hand movements over the weather map. The court ruled that pointing at clouds was not creative enough to be protected.

fakes.name: The doorbell tune
fakes.fact: A German songwriter sued a doorbell maker because its “ding-dong” tune copied four notes from his 1980s pop song. The court agreed, and thousands of doorbells had to be reprogrammed.

fakes.name: The crying-laughing emoji
fakes.fact: In 2018 a Korean illustrator sued a messaging app, claiming its laughing-crying face copied a sticker he drew in 2008. The court ruled that a face with tears is too simple to own.

fakes.name: The poetic shopping list
fakes.fact: A French novelist's family sued an auction house for selling his handwritten shopping lists. The court agreed that one list, written in rhyme, was literature and protected by copyright.

fakes.name: The hold music
fakes.fact: In 2016 a Canadian musician found out that a bank had used his song as telephone hold music for nine years. A court ordered the bank to pay him for every hour callers had waited.

fake: Give it a short name, like a newspaper headline: “The ___ case”.
A kind of person (a songwriter, an artist) against a kind of company, in a real country.
Something weird but possible: a sound, a dance, a photo, a few notes.
One or two steps: who noticed, and how it got to court.
Who won, and the judge's reason in one sentence.
A year, an amount of money or how many things had to change.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“they only won half the money”): perfect things sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
